items.title: Investigate Trump Like a Mob Boss
items.description: I f you are looking for government corruption, Washington has always been a target-rich environment. But the past two years of the Trump administration have seen the swamp rise to extraordinary levels. Despite remarkable threats from the White House suggesting that congressional investigations might be a crime , Democrats are preparing to scrutinize what Senator Raphael Warnock has called “the most corrupt administration in American history.” Many Democrats will be tempted to go directly after the president for his misdeeds. A better strategy would be to take a page from the prosecutor’s playbook on investigating organized crime. In many ways Trump and his inner circle resemble an organized crime family, with Donald as the don. Such groups are tightly knit, held together by bonds of unwavering loyalty to the organization and its authoritarian leader. They prize secrecy. They enforce their demands through intimidation and coercion. The members work to enrich themselves, displaying little regard for law or institutions. Responsibilities are compartmentalized and diffuse, in ways that insulate those at the top from accountability. When prosecutors work to dismantle these organizations, they often start from the bottom: find the lower-level players, build cases against them, persuade them to cooperate, then work up the ladder. [ Quinta Jurecic: A very suspicious prosecution of two former FBI officials ] But expecting Attorney General Todd Blanche to pursue such cases would be like expecting the consigliere to investigate the family. He almost certainly won’t appoint special counsels to investigate, even though a squadron of them is called for. And Trump has already promised to pardon everyone “who has come within 200 feet” of the Oval Office. Given the zeal with which he wields the pardon power, anyone whose dreams of accountability feature perp walks and orange jumpsuits is likely to be disappointed. Congress might also be tempted to impeach Trump, as it did twice during his first term. But Democrats would be wise to avoid that route this time. Presidential impeachment sucks all the air out of the room. It feeds Trump’s martyr complex and keeps him at the center of attention. And although it might satisfy some Democrats, in the end it will almost certainly fail again. In the new Senate, more than 10 Republican senators would have to vote to convict. Even after such a decisive electoral rebuke, it’s hard to see that happening. The more fruitful course for Democrats will be to leave Trump to his interior decorating and recognize that their time is better spent focusing on the misconduct of those around him and those tied to his administration. In the process, they will inevitably document the misconduct of Trump himself. Congressional-oversight investigations are now more crucial than ever. In this environment, they are the best available vehicle for exposing and documenting the administration’s misconduct. And unlike with a criminal grand jury, congressional investigations can be open to the public, which is essential for informing the public’s vote, come 2028. Congress can build a public record of the transgressions of this administration, working all the way up to Trump himself, for all of America to see. T he coming congressional investigations will face unprecedented hurdles. But Congress possesses many of the same investigative tools that a prosecutor would use to build a case against a crime boss and his organization. Congressional committees are busy staffing up with attorneys and investigators, many of whom resigned or were forced out of Blanche’s DOJ, who know how to do this work. First, as Senator Ron Wyden so succinctly posted on X : “Subpoenas.” Like a prosecutor conducting a grand-jury investigation, Congress can compel the production of documents and the testimony of witnesses under oath. While in the minority, Democrats could only request information, and had no way to force compliance. That will now change. Congress, like a prosecutor, also has the power to grant immunity to a witness who claims a Fifth Amendment right not to testify. For a witness, a grant of immunity is an offer you can’t refuse: It requires you to testify or face contempt charges. As a former federal prosecutor, I’ve seen firsthand the power of immunity in unearthing the truth. Congress is often reluctant to grant immunity for fear of undermining a potential criminal prosecution of the immunized witness. But that is less of a concern if one assumes that Trump will pardon the witness anyway. If people defy subpoenas, Congress can go to court to enforce them, and it should do so aggressively, asking judges to fast-track the process. Courts can move quickly when they need to. Stonewalling should not be tolerated or rewarded. Although we can expect the administration and those closest to Trump to resist at every turn, private companies and individuals have a great deal of relevant information and will likely be more compliant. These are the lower rungs on the ladder that can lead to further evidence and investigation. Congress can also vote to hold witnesses in contempt. Under current law, a contempt resolution would be referred to the Justice Department for potential prosecution and thus would go nowhere. But there is a five-year statute of limitations, and prosecutions would still be potentially viable if there is a Democratic administration after 2028. That’s also true for any potential charges for witnesses who lie before Congress or obstruct an investigation. Of course, an ordinary mob boss doesn’t have the pardon power. Trump’s ability to pardon the malefactors who surround him will loom over this process. But pardons do not excuse a witness from testifying before Congress. Indeed, a preemptive pardon could make it more challenging for a witness to invoke the Fifth Amendment, because he or she will no longer have a well-founded fear of prosecution. [ Read: Trump can prosecute anyone now ] Pardons also don’t shield a witness from public shame. They don’t foreclose potential civil liability or other business or professional consequences. And a pardon can’t stop Congress from impeaching and removing a Cabinet member or other presidential appointee. In addition, at least some witnesses will have to make a difficult calculation: Am I really willing to commit (further) crimes and stake my liberty on the promise of a pardon from an erratic and unfocused president? Who would want to take that bet? In this particular investigation, the don himself will likely remain out of reach—at least where criminal liability is concerned. Given the Supreme Court’s decision on presidential immunity, even if investigations uncover criminal conduct by Trump, prosecuting that conduct after he leaves office is likely to be a nonstarter. And although the validity of such a move is untested, he’ll probably pardon himself on the way out the door as additional insurance. But Congress can ensure that he does not escape the judgment of history. This historic election is a mandate for Congress to lead a similarly historic public reckoning. It must vigorously investigate the corruption and misconduct of the past two years. Not because those investigations will lead to criminal prosecutions. Not because the mission is to “get” Trump. But because Congress has an obligation to build a historical record of what has happened, hold those involved publicly accountable, and enact legislation designed to ensure that it can’t happen again.

items.title: 30 Years for Moving a Box
items.description: D aniel Sanchez was driving his pickup truck through a college town in North Texas on a Sunday afternoon last summer when he noticed the glow of bright blue police lights behind him. As he pulled over, he realized it wasn’t one or two squad cars; it was half a dozen. Police officers rushed to his door, guns pointed at him. “I thought that I was going to die,” he told me. “Like, honestly, when I saw the amount of cops around me and the guns, I’m like, Oh, whoa, what is this? ” Sanchez was patted down, his arms cuffed behind him as an officer guided him into the back of a police vehicle. Born in Mexico, Sanchez came to the United States as a teenager and was undocumented for many years but later obtained a green card. As he sat in the backseat, “Always on Time” by Ja Rule played on the radio. An officer opened the door and repeatedly asked whether he had any explosives in his truck. No one would tell him why he was being arrested. About 36 hours earlier, a police officer had been shot and injured outside the Prairieland Detention Center 60 miles away. What had started as a July 4 demonstration by a group of protesters shooting off fireworks had become the scene of a violent attack on the officer, who was airlifted from the scene but survived. Law enforcement flooded the area, arresting anyone involved, then widened their search. Ten people were already in custody—Sanchez’s wife was among them—but the shooter was still at large. Sanchez, though, hadn’t been at the ICE detention center that night. He told me he hadn’t even been aware of the plans or that his wife was going. The couple had gotten into a fight earlier that week, and he had been staying at his parents’ house. At the time of his arrest, he was still trying to piece together what had happened, what his wife had done, and how much trouble she was in. FBI agents had been watching him that morning, and they had been listening in when his wife called him from jail, frantically telling him to hire a lawyer and to possibly adopt her daughter. “I’m scared of the proximity for you,” she had told him. Soon after that call ended, the agents photographed Sanchez as he carried a taped-up box out of his parents’ house and placed it into his truck bed. They followed him as he drove nearly 50 miles northwest to an apartment complex in Denton and left the box outside a door on the second floor. Law enforcement didn’t have a warrant for his arrest, so officers continued to follow him and looked for a reason to pull him over. Eventually he made what they considered a wide right turn. Sanchez was taken to a holding facility. Even though he had provided his identification to police, he was listed for two days as John Doe while his family tried to locate him. And what about that box? It had been taken inside the apartment, and nearly six hours later, investigators obtained a warrant to seize it. Armored vehicles pulled up to the apartment complex, and agents threw a flash-bang and broke through the front door, which one tenant later described as “something like you’d see in Fallujah.” The agents found Sanchez’s box in a closet. There were no explosives inside, no guns, nothing directly connected to the protest that had turned violent. The items later submitted as evidence include several dozen political booklets on a variety of topics that prosecutors claimed ideologically tied Sanchez to the shooting. One of the titles was War in the Streets: Tactical Lessons From the Global Civil War Vol. 1. One was a “primer for the criminally-minded anarchist.” One that the prosecution would point to during the trial was called Insurgency: An Anarchist Journal of Total Destruction . The box also contained some of Sanchez’s artwork. One drawing shows a skull inside a police helmet with a flower growing out of it, and text that reads From their ashes we shall rise . It also has the letters ACAB , which stand for “All Cops Are Bastards.” Other pieces promote “animal liberation,” depicting a masked person cradling a bunny or a masked raccoon holding shears. Another sketch has Donald Trump in a red tie, his face colored like a clown’s, with three swastikas around him. The most shocking illustration in the box shows four versions of Trump hanged by a noose; in two of them, he holds a sign reading Hang in There , with cats clinging to a rope. Source: U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Texas These are some of the contents of the box that the U.S. Attorney’s Office submitted as evidence during the trial. Although there was nothing illegal about making such artwork or possessing the booklets, prosecutors claimed that Sanchez moved the box as part of a conspiracy to protect his wife. They accused him and other defendants of being part of a North Texas cell of antifa, considered a terrorist group by the Trump administration. Although many of the cases that the administration has tried to bring against anti-ICE protesters elsewhere in the country have fallen apart before going to trial, the Prairieland case proceeded. Defense attorneys for Sanchez and others had been so convinced that their clients would not be convicted that they didn’t call any witnesses. But after a three-week trial that concluded in March, a jury found all nine defendants guilty. A judge then classified the convicted men and women as terrorists, and imposed sentences to match. The gunman who injured the police officer was sentenced to 100 years in prison. Sanchez’s wife, who helped organize the protest, was given 70 years. Sanchez got 30 years. As I tried to understand this sentence, I combed through Sanchez’s phone records, and the geolocation data on his phone. I went through hundreds of photos from the government exhibits, reviewing materials that were collected but never discussed at trial. I talked with Sanchez for more than six hours across more than two dozen prison phone calls, and he never came across as defensive, but I looked for evidence that he might have been hiding something. I figured something really bad must have been in that box, and I just hadn’t seen it yet. Or, alternatively, that Sanchez must have had some bigger role in the events than what had been reported. But I found no hidden explanation for what had happened to him. As best as I could establish, Sanchez is set to spend the next 30 years in prison simply for moving a box of radical zines. F or years , Sanchez was active at protests. He eagerly collected leftist political magazines—including more innocuous titles about canning and fermentation or race and gender inequality, and more radical ones about avoiding surveillance or engaging in confrontational protest—and he participated in a book club named after the anarchist Emma Goldman. Growing up in both Mexico and Texas, Sanchez, who is 40 and goes by Des and Dani, liked to make funny artwork that caused viewers to look twice. As a teenager, influenced by the writings of Che Guevara , he began leaving graffiti in gentrified neighborhoods as a critique of profit-driven developers. He had a punk-goth style, a distrust of police, and a distaste for cruelty toward animals, and he came to define his views as anarchist. In his early 30s, he met Maricela Rueda, a poet who shared his politics. They were both artistic and creative, emotional and expressive. They married in 2020; she would become a doula, and he became a father figure for her young daughter. Several years ago, Sanchez receded from the book club after he had a falling out with some of the members, and began spending more time on his art. He had taught himself to tattoo using materials he ordered online, and he and two close friends—brothers who go by the names Dro and Kilo—had just opened their own studio. He sought to make his art relatable and accessible. He studied children’s books for inspiration and infused his work with playful animals—while keeping a focus on politics. A 2024 campaign to raise awareness of banned books featured a vinyl sticker he made of a possum reading Art Spiegelman’s Maus , with text around it reading Trash Fascism, Not Books . When Trump returned to the White House, so too did Sanchez’s dismay over immigration policies that brought enforcement officers into cities to arrest as many people as possible. Sanchez had once worked as a teacher’s assistant in an elementary school, and he had seen how attendance dwindled when families worried about raids. “There are kids that will not see their parents come back from work,” he wrote on Instagram, adding that he wasn’t afraid to lose clients or friends who supported Trump and his immigration policies. [ From the November issue: The babies left behind in America ] Sanchez’s wife was also angry. Just before July 4, 2025, Rueda told her friends that she wanted to organize a protest. She was frustrated at work. “Can we burn it all down?” she wrote in a small-group chat that did not include her husband. She proposed a demonstration at the detention facility to attract attention and support the detainees inside. Plans spread through Signal group chats. Some participants were part of the Socialist Rifle Association and had spent time training with firearms and learning tactical maneuvers from Benjamin Song, an activist and former Marine Corps reservist. On Independence Day, protesters gathered outside the Prairieland facility. They wore black clothing and masks. Some turned off their cellphones or put them in metallic-lined bags that blocked tracking services. One protester had a red cooler with fireworks in it. Others had backpacks with water, snacks, and first-aid kits to treat life-threatening traumatic injuries. Many had guns but some left them in their cars. As fireworks exploded in the air that night, Rueda shouted into a megaphone a phrase that translates to hope: “ ¡Esperanza! ” A little after 10:30 p.m., two of the protesters peeled away to vandalize vehicles in the parking lot and spray-paint an unmanned guard shack: Fuck you pigs . A detention-center employee ordered them to leave, and some protesters began to comply. Another employee called the police, reporting that someone was trying to get into the facility. Alvarado police Lieutenant Thomas Gross sped over, jumped from his car with his Glock 9-mm drawn, and saw a figure dressed in all black and a neon-green face mask holding an AR-15-style rifle. As Gross ran toward the figure and yelled “Get on the ground,” there were bursts of gunfire. Gross collapsed and screamed, “I’m hit!” A bullet struck him near his neck. He was briefly hospitalized as law enforcement began to hunt for the shooter, later identified as Song. Song had encouraged others to carry firearms, and he alarmed some of them when he suggested the night before the protest that they break into the facility to free some of the detainees, an idea that did not gather support, according to testimony from one of those who pleaded guilty. One of the defendants later told the FBI she suspected that Song had intentionally shot the officer “in cold blood” and used the group of activists as “cover while he gets the fuck away.” Song avoided arrest for 11 days. Police stopped other protesters as they tried to leave, and they found firearms and body armor in several cars. “This is like a targeted hit on Prairieland,” one officer remarked to another, an exchange captured in body-camera footage. Sanchez told me he barely knew Song and was unaware of all of this. He had been staying with his parents in Garland since the argument with his wife earlier in the week, which he would not detail for me other than to say it was “personal stuff” and unrelated to what later happened at Prairieland. “Dani had nothing to do with it,” Rueda told me in a brief call she made from prison after I wrote her a letter. “Dani was not invited.” When I asked her why, she responded, “We have different friends.” So that night, as she was shouting outside the detention center, he was an hour’s drive away with a group of his friends at an AMC movie theater, watching 28 Years Later while eating popcorn and drinking a Coca-Cola Cherry slushie. He told me he didn’t even know that the detention center existed. B y morning , when the shooting was starting to hit the news, Sanchez told me he was still unaware of it. He called his wife around noon, but she didn’t pick up. He drove to their house and didn’t see her car, so went inside to let the dog out and tend to their cats and rabbits. She tried calling him from jail, but the call didn’t go through. Rueda called her mother and, in Spanish, said “something terrible has happened” and that they needed to find an attorney. She said she couldn’t get into details on the phone but urged her to reach out to Sanchez so he could find out more information from “the community.” She said in the call that Sanchez was not involved. But to law enforcement, her insistence that her mother reach Sanchez made it sound like he could be. Sanchez told me that he drove to Rueda’s mother’s house, where they discussed finding a lawyer, then returned for nearly two hours to the house he shared with Rueda. I asked him several times whether he moved anything from the home at that time, and he said no: “They’re trying to say that I took stuff out of there, like so-called evidence. And it’s just ridiculous.” Prosecutors later suggested, without providing any proof, that he could have taken material away from the home, because investigators’ subsequent searches there failed to turn up the incriminating materials they’d found in the homes of others. That evening, on Sanchez’s way back to his parents’ house, he stopped by his tattoo shop and asked to speak with his co-owners in the back. He soon began sobbing inconsolably. “I have never seen him so serious in his life,” Kilo told me. “He seemed really scared and like he didn’t know what to do.” They talked through ways to help, but they also urged him to keep his distance. “We were like, Dude, you can’t do anything. Stay away. Once it’s that big, you don’t want to risk anything ,” Kilo said. [ Read: What the Prairieland prosecutions reveal about Trump’s America ] That evening, Sanchez prayed and burned incense. After a sleepless night, the phone rang at 10:55 a.m., and the operator asked if he would take a call from the Johnson County Jail. Seconds later his wife was on the line. “I don’t know what the fuck happened. Like, I can’t believe that that would have happened,” she said, according to a recording later entered into evidence. “Everybody’s life is fucking ruined because they’re gonna fucking put us on parade.” Police were listening in on the call, and four officers from an FBI surveillance team were outside Sanchez’s parents’ house. About 30 minutes after hanging up, FBI agents watched from a distance as Sanchez loaded the cardboard box into his 2012 white Chevrolet Silverado. Sanchez told me that the political zines in the box had been there for years, but that it didn’t seem wise to hold on to them now “because at any point, immigration can show up at your house.” He insists he wasn’t trying to cover up anything related to his wife, that everything in the box was his. Illustration by Medar de la Cruz The prior day, he had been in touch with Kelsey Fryman, a longtime friend who was part of the book club. Sanchez was nervous that law enforcement could come after him. “I mean, his wife is being called a terrorist for attending a protest. He is an immigrant dealing with the Trump administration’s immigration policies,” she told me. She urged him not to throw away the materials in the box and to bring them to her instead. “I was like, A chance for some artwork and some zines? Sign me up ,” she told me. Looking through the items, it’s clear why Sanchez worried they were problematic. But it’s also hard to see how having radical pamphlets and artwork merited his prosecution. “It’s literature!” Fryman told me. “Political literature is supposed to be protected under the First Amendment. How is giving a friend political literature a crime?” T wo months after the shooting in Prairieland , the conservative activist Charlie Kirk was assassinated, and Trump and Stephen Miller—then a top aide who has since become the president’s chief of staff—declared war on liberals. Antifa generally refers to the decentralized movement of left-wing protesters who organize regionally and oppose some combination of facism, capitalism, and the mainstream political parties. But in Miller’s rendering, antifa was a fully formed militant organization with a hierarchy and leadership structure that experts say does not actually exist. “With God as my witness, we are going to use every resource we have at the Department of Justice, Homeland Security, and throughout this government to identify, disrupt, dismantle, and destroy these networks,” Miller said. Soon after that, Trump signed an executive order designating antifa as a domestic-terrorist organization. Then he signed a memorandum urging DOJ to prosecute crimes committed by antifa members “to the maximum extent permissible by law.” The Prairieland case was an opportunity to do so. [ Read: A chief of staff who ‘will crack skulls’ ] The defendants were collectively branded the “North Texas Antifa Cell.” Prosecutors added new terrorism charges, accusing the group of being part of “a militant enterprise.” Seven defendants agreed to plea deals, which involved admitting guilt and signing declarations that those in the group adhered to anti-fascist ideologies. Sanchez told me that he was offered several plea deals but rejected them all. Prosecutors initially said he could plead guilty to tampering with evidence in exchange for a 10-year sentence and agreeing that he was part of a terrorist organization. Then they dropped the latter condition. Months later they said they’d add more charges if he didn’t agree. When he declined, he said, they added a conspiracy charge. Later, their offer dropped to five years. A guilty plea, however, would mean losing his green card and getting deported. “I’m like, No, this is my home, ” he told me. Besides, he said, “I’m not going to sign that away because I didn’t do anything.” Around Thanksgiving, a procedural error led to Sanchez being freed for eight days. He visited the wildlife center where he had volunteered, and held baby opossums and raccoons. He went to the mall, attended his nephew’s piano recital, and listened to KPop Demon Hunters music. His family and friends had a celebration combining Christmas, Thanksgiving, New Year’s, and his birthday all at once. His mom made vegan pozole, and a friend gave him a tattoo on his right wrist: No one is illegal. And then, when the mistake was confirmed, he returned to jail. His brief bit of freedom occurred as the legal threats were growing. A superseding indictment combined his case with those of the protesters who were at Prairieland so they could be tried as a group. This approach allowed prosecutors to broaden the scope of who could be tied to the crime, the same way investigations into an international terrorist network implicate not just those who commit violence but those who fund the network and materially support its ideology. Jeffrey Breinholt, the former deputy chief in the DOJ’s counterterrorism section, helped pioneer the use of such laws after 9/11. But in the Prairieland case, there was not the same type of well-established group with a defined, shared ideology. And prosecutors were using some of the most aggressive tools at their disposal to target those who showed up at an event to express dissent with government policies, even if they didn’t destroy property or hurt anyone. “I think this is way out of line,” Breinholt told me. The principles of jurisprudence that he helped establish, he said, “are being misused now for political purposes.” During the trial in March, prosecutors tried to paint the entire group as violent. Even if some members had left their weapons in their cars, they still had spent years promoting the idea of anarchy. The prosecution pointed to some of Sanchez’s anti-police artwork to suggest that the group opposed law enforcement. Kasey Bennett, an FBI special agent who focuses on domestic and international terrorism and weapons of mass destruction, testified that although possessing such materials is legal, they show “a joint ideology.” This was the closest explanation I have found for why Sanchez was deemed guilty: He knew some of the people who were there and shared similar beliefs. The materials in this box, prosecutors argued, helped show motive and intent for the attack. Bennett testified that, because similar political pamphlets were found in the possession of several of the defendants, it indicated a connection between them. “And when a number of people are involved in something, what do we typically call that?” a prosecutor asked Bennett in court. The agent responded: “a conspiracy.” The government’s reasoning prompted broad condemnation from civil-rights, free-speech, immigration, and legal organizations. On cross-examination, Sanchez’s lawyer emphasized that none of the items were illegal to own, and none were related to the shooting. It was true that Sanchez knew some of the other protesters. He was married to one of them, after all. But others questioned during the trial said they had never seen him before. One said that the first time he met Sanchez was when they were in jail awaiting trial. To enhance charges of a conspiracy, prosecutors pointed to some of the materials in the box that could have been Rueda’s, including a letter from a child addressed to “Mrs. Sanchez.” It was a thank-you note for teaching a hip-hop class, Sanchez told me, something that he did before he met his wife, who did not take his last name. “The kid does not know how to spell, unfortunately,” Sanchez said. I pressed Sanchez on some of his artwork that appears to depict vandalism and violence. “All of it is satire,” he insisted. Some of it, he conceded, is “a little raw and pretty shocking.” He mentioned an ICE vehicle in flames, and pointed to the butterflies emerging from it as a commentary that something beautiful could emerge if hard-line immigration policies were abolished. “It doesn’t mean that I’m encouraging people to do anything.” [ Read: ICE after the blowout ] I also pressed him on his four-panel drawing of Trump in a noose. This wasn’t discussed at trial but was included in the government exhibits. He had been trying to riff on a 2009 Banksy work called Hanging Klansman . They were sketches on scrap paper, he said. “It never developed anything, you know? So it just stayed on that piece of paper.” Sanchez considers himself an anti-fascist but told me that it’s “absurd” for him to be considered a member of antifa. “It’s a label for something that is not real. They’re trying to label something and create an organization of something that is not an organization.” The prosecution rested after nearly three weeks of trial. Defense attorneys were so confident they did not see a need to call their own witnesses and moved to closing arguments, a common legal strategy. Christopher Weinbel, a public defender and one of Sanchez’s lawyers, argued that Sanchez had moved the box not as part of a cover-up, but “because he didn’t want to be involved.” “We don’t lose our freedom when we move our own belongings. We don’t lose our freedom when our friends and family get arrested,” Weinbel said in closing. “Alexander Hamilton said the practice of arbitrary imprisonments is the favorite instrument of tyranny. That’s what’s happening.” D uring the trial , Sanchez recalled, the defendants were treated like the terrorists they were accused of being. They were transported to the heavily secured courthouse each day in something that resembled a military convoy. They were moved in wheelchairs, with their hands cuffed behind them and their ankles locked to the chairs. In the courtroom, they were told by the marshals not to make eye contact or wave at their family members. “We just had to be catatonic the whole time,” Sanchez said, “just like, try not to express any emotions.” The jury deliberated for two days and reached its verdicts on a Friday afternoon ahead of the local school system’s spring break. The judge read each of the verdicts aloud; Sanchez’s came last. We, the jury, find the defendant, Daniel Rolando Sanchez Estrada, guilty. Nearly everyone was found guilty on nearly all charges. For Sanchez that included charges of concealing documents and, along with his wife, conspiracy to conceal documents. The only sounds in the room were people crying. “Everybody immediately thought, you know, it’s like their lives are ended,” he told me. Afterward, Sanchez called his sister and his mom, who were in the car together. His sister remembers him screaming: Why did this happen? How did this happen? I didn’t do anything. I didn’t do anything. I shouldn’t be here. I shouldn’t be here . In the background, his sister recalled, she could hear other defendants wailing in sounds that haunt her. “They were all in disbelief,” she said. When I brought up the moment with Sanchez, who is nearly always composed and even jovial, he became emotional. Three months later, everyone was sentenced. Song, the shooter, received 100 years. Most others got 50 years. The numbers were outside of recent norms. The average prison sentence for a domestic-terrorism attack that resulted in at least one person being injured but no deaths—which is what occurred at Prairieland—was 8.6 years, according to an analysis of criminal convictions from 2014 to 2019 by the National Consortium for the Study of Terrorism and Responses to Terrorism. Judge Reed O’Connor, the chief judge of the Northern District of Texas, oversees one of the most conservative jurisdictions in the country. Nearly every judge was appointed by a Republican president, and decisions tend to be upheld by the Fifth Circuit, considered the most conservative appellate court. During his sentencing hearing, Sanchez told the judge about his love of literature, art, and education. Some of his art can be raw and controversial, he said, but it’s how he performs his activism. He mentioned having read Benjamin Franklin’s autobiography while in jail, how the Founding Father’s writings and pamphlets were controversial, too, but they were protected. “I believe in a world where many worlds can fit together, and we take care of each other, and we help each other overcome whatever adversities and challenges we have,” he said. “I’m a father. I am a husband, I’m a teacher. I’m an artist. A poet. I am many things, Your Honor, but I am not a terrorist.” The presentencing recommendation for a nonviolent offense and a first-time offender was 10 to 16 months. But Frank Gatto, an assistant U.S. attorney, said that Sanchez should receive a harsher sentence. “He’s part of this same community. He shares in their beliefs. He shares in their ideology. He shares in their disagreements with government policy,” he told the judge. Sanchez’s lawyer argued that this was ridiculous. Such sentences should be reserved for ISIS recruiters. Hardened criminals. Murderers. Not for someone who moved a box of his own materials, none of which were illegal. Those appeals did little to sway O’Connor, who treated Sanchez as if he were a career violent offender and put his crime into a category more significant than hijacking an airplane. O’Connor also used his judicial discretion to order that the sentences be served consecutively rather than concurrently. He said that although he understood Sanchez’s argument, his movement of the box “was part of a cleanup operation” after “a terrorist attack.” A 30-year sentence was appropriate. “It serves to deter others from this kind of conduct, ensures just punishment,” he said. With his decision final, the proceedings concluded and the judge remarked: “Good luck to you, sir.” Over several months, I kept wondering if I was missing something. Had some of the materials that Sanchez moved actually belonged to his wife? Was he trying to conceal evidence? Had he kept in closer touch with those who were at the protest than he had admitted? I found nothing to support any of these possibilities, but neither could I definitively rule them out. Even so, it was hard to understand how he deserved a 30-year sentence. Illustration by Medar de la Cruz [ Read: In Trump immigration cases, it’s one thing in public, another in court ] I reached out to Gatto, the U.S. attorney who tried the case, but he didn’t return my messages. I tried O’Connor and Judge Mark T. Pittman, who oversaw the trial. They declined to talk. The names of jurors are not public, and I couldn’t find any who had identified themselves. I asked the White House whether Miller, who pressed for the framework that was used to convict Sanchez, would talk, but instead received a statement: “President Trump has made it clear: Antifa terrorists and their networks will be investigated and prosecuted to the fullest extent of the law.” Attorney General Todd Blanche and FBI Director Kash Patel—who both issued statements praising the sentences—also declined requests to talk about the case. (A DOJ spokesperson said in a statement that Sanchez and others “were afforded every right of due process” and that “the court handed down sentences that were appropriate given the guidelines and reflected the seriousness of these crimes.”) I had hoped to hear from the police officer who was shot, but he also did not return my messages. Sanchez’s family is now waiting on an appeal, but it could be two years before it gets taken up in the Fifth Circuit. His parents took in the shar-pei-bulldog mix he was set to adopt. He has been calling his teenage stepdaughter, who is living with her biological father, and gotten reports on the new Spider-Man movie. His friends have kept the tattoo shop running. His sister, a bookstore owner, added a section for banned books and is trying to figure out how to file his taxes. In the aftermath of Prairieland, the Trump administration has tried to use a similar approach in a number of other cases, with mixed or incomplete results, in Washington, Illinois, and Minnesota. Xavier T. de Janon, the executive director of the National Lawyers Guild, told me that it is hard to undersell the significance of the Prairieland case. It should serve as a wake-up call, he said, for any American who believes that democratic rights are protected and prosecutions have their limits. “I don’t know if it’s rational to say that anymore,” he said. S anchez is now prisoner No. 95099-511 . I spent weeks attempting to meet with him at a medium-security prison complex in Victorville, California. It is the same one that once housed John Walker Lindh, who was sentenced to 20 years after pleading guilty to aiding the Taliban. Despite Sanchez agreeing, the warden denied my request, under a broad provision in the regulations that “the interview would probably cause serious unrest or disturb the good order of the institution.” I asked whether I could come during normal visiting hours, or make other accommodations, but was denied without explanation. Sanchez is allotted 15 minutes of phone time a day, so we began a series of truncated calls spanning three months. Some days the prison went on lockdown and I wouldn’t hear from him at our appointed time. Other days he could make several calls, but there had to be a gap of 30 minutes between each. In his section of the prison there were only six phones for more than 100 inmates, he told me, so he would get in line again and again. He was remarkably calm and measured, asking about my weekends at the start of a call and often ending with a cheery, “Blessings!” He has been working in the library and offers book recommendations to other inmates, and noted that the prison collection includes George Orwell’s 1984 . Interspersed among the romance novels, religious texts, and Westerns, he has checked out books that would not have been out of place in the box that he moved: Feminism, Film, and Fascism ; The Handmaid’s Tale ; and Animal Liberation . One day he noticed that The Week magazine featured an illustration of Trump with a voting box on fire—an image not too different from ones he used to create. He has been drawing again, sticking mostly to animals and flowers—nothing political. He has been writing poetry that he reads over the phone with a delivery fitting of a slam session. Most of his fellow inmates, who have long sentences and a history of felonies, think he is strange, especially when he attempts to continue his vegan diet. “They see me coming in, and they’re like, What are you in for? And I’m like, Oh, books. ” He chuckled a bit in disbelief. “It’s completely wild. Honestly, it seems surreal. If it wasn’t so cruel, it would be laughable and ridiculous,” he said. “But I’m in here.” In our six hours of conversations, he seemed remarkably at peace. He professed no regrets about any of his actions over those few days last year, or not fleeing when he had a chance, or not taking the plea deals placed in front of him. He hasn’t lost hope that his appeal will succeed or a future president might issue a pardon. But he grew tearful at what it would be like to be released from prison—reunited with his family, vegan tacos, and his motorcycle—only to be deported to Mexico. In prison, he tries to find small pleasures—waking up to the smell of rain, his morning cup of instant coffee. Sometimes the scene outside the brutalist-style facility reminds him of the movie Dune . He takes note of the pigeons and crows hoping for scraps near the cafeteria, and he relishes his brief moments outside and reading by the lamp in his cell. But each day, he tells me, when the steel door slams shut and there’s a loud click from a key turning the lock, time stops—and the heaviness of his situation hits anew.

items.title: The Only Thing Nathan Fielder Won’t Show
items.description: Y ou Can See Everything has given America a new villain: Billy Evans. The blockbuster documentary, created by Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim, is about Elizabeth Holmes, the former CEO of the blood-test company Theranos, and the days before she reports to federal prison after being convicted of fraud. But Evans, her partner and the father of her two children, manages to come out of the film looking worse than she does—not because he committed any crime, but because he wanted to get paid for participating in the documentary. The documentary stages a reenactment of a scene in which Evans negotiates with Fielder and Oppenheim and some A24 executives. Evans is letting a film crew into his home. He’s letting them record his children. He’s even letting them record him in the shower. That degree of access has clear monetary value. But the executives react as if no one in history has ever suggested such an untoward thing. Evans insists, and they begrudgingly agree. The film spends much of its second half interrogating Holmes and Evans’s financial motive, and what that reveals about their honesty and transparency (though a title card at the end reveals that Evans gave up his profit share before the film was released after all). I get why viewers would find the idea objectionable: How dare Evans and Holmes profit from a documentary that exists only because she was convicted of a crime? Reason called the deal a “crooked bargain.” The Los Angeles Times explained to readers that paying documentary subjects is unusual under “traditional journalistic standards.” It is, of course, true that introducing a pay-to-play dynamic to a truth-seeking mission has the potential to warp the incentives of everyone involved. But all of this is more complicated than it appears. For a film devoted to questioning both the honesty and transparency of its subjects and of the project of filmmaking itself, it’s surprising how little scrutiny this central plot point has received. [ Read: How did Nathan Fielder pull this off? ] I, too, have sat in front of documentary cameras in studios. I’ve invited filmmakers and journalists and photographers into my home maybe a dozen times. But these occasions are the exception. I have no idea how many nonconsensual photographs have been taken of me since I was first arrested in Italy in 2007 on the murder charge that took me more than seven years to beat. I wouldn’t be surprised if that number topped 1 million. Thousands of these photos are available for licensing. On Getty Images alone, a search for my name returns nearly 5,000 results. These pictures are of my face, but they are other people’s property. If I want one of these photos of myself, I have to pay for it like anyone else. What I’ve learned is that standards of journalistic integrity can be used to ensure that, in cases of “public interest,” money flows to everyone but the “person of interest.” Earlier this year, Hulu released a documentary directed by my husband, Christopher Robinson, called Mouth of the Wolf: Amanda Knox Returns to Italy . It’s an intimate film about my attempts to reconcile with the Italians who misunderstood me, the media that vilified me, and, most of all, the prosecutor who threw me in prison and later agreed to meet with me. To tell this story, Christopher had to provide some background on the case, which required licensing images and footage of me as a 21-year-old on trial for murder. He also wanted to convey the ongoing media trauma I was confronting by returning to Italy. On my first trip back, in 2019, the paparazzi swarmed me at the airport, shouting my name, clambering over one another to get at me as Christopher helped me into a car. One tripped and fell to the pavement. I didn’t love the idea of funneling money toward some of the very people who’d traumatized me, but one photo in particular—of Christopher shielding my face inside the car while the paparazzo is reflected in the window—was too evocative not to include. We paid Reuters $408 to license the photo. The Atlantic paid $75 to include it in this article. I don’t know what the photographer received. (Daniele Mascolo / Reuters) One of Christopher’s primary motivations to make this film was to reveal the version of me he knew—the wife and mother struggling to make sense of her past, as opposed to the “public figure,” the subject of a true-crime story that had been told many times before. In 2016, Netflix had released a documentary about my case. I gave the filmmakers hours of interviews. I invited them into my home—basically a run-down shack where I lived alone with four cats—and gave them access to a trove of personal archival material they couldn’t have obtained anywhere else. I wasn’t paid for any of that, though countless people have assumed, and suggested to my face, that I was richly compensated. Judging by the film’s success (including two Emmy nominations), plenty of people saw monetary returns on that creative effort. I was not one of them. At the time, I was told that the rule was that documentary subjects couldn’t be paid, and that the rule protected the film’s integrity. I believed it. When a friend told me afterward that I should have been compensated, I remember thinking that he just didn’t understand how documentaries worked. What I know now, after years of working in film and television myself, is that subjects get paid all the time; they just don’t get paid as subjects . A production licenses their home videos; a studio options the rights to their memoir, or hires the subjects as consultants. Everyone in the television and film industry knows of these arrangements, but almost no one explains them to the person whose life is on camera, who is usually the least experienced and most desperate person at the table. Today, when someone—in many cases, a wrongly convicted person—comes to me for advice because a documentary filmmaker has approached them, the first thing I say is: Get paid. Don’t give away your family photos for free. Write your story down and self-publish it so the studio can purchase the IP. Very few people in the film industry actually believe that money corrupts a documentary. If they did, they wouldn’t have built so many loopholes for money to slip through. What they do believe is that openness about money corrupts the appearance of integrity. The “traditional journalistic standards” are there to manipulate the audience’s impression of a film. These standards are by no means culturally universal. I’ve been on Good Morning America many times over the years. ABC has never paid me for an appearance. I’ve also been on Good Morning Britain , which has paid me for my time. Same type of show, same kind of segment, same person on the couch. It’s a bit like tipping at a restaurant: In the United States, it’s expected that you add 20 percent to the bill for the service. In Japan, leaving a tip is often seen as an insult. In Britain, it’s more common for TV guests to be compensated for their time and exclusivity, and many documentary filmmakers pay “disturbance fees” for the inconvenience of filming in people’s homes and workplaces. Although these countries do have very different approaches to press freedom that affect how journalism is carried out, in many cases the custom tells you a lot more about the culture than about the ethics. [ Amanda Knox: Who owns Amanda Knox? ] The best argument against paying documentary subjects is that doing so motivates them to say what sells, to become the character the film needs. In my experience, however, money is rarely the biggest incentive for the subject. When I was interviewed for the Netflix documentary, I did so without compensation because I had something far more valuable at stake. I was being retried in absentia for the crime I’d already been acquitted of, I was facing potential extradition, and I worried that it might be my last chance to tell my side of the story. I desperately wanted to be believed, to be seen and judged for who I really was. I was about as motivated as a subject could be, and nobody paid me anything. E very subject walks in with stakes. So does every filmmaker. A film maintains its integrity by acknowledging both. Christopher opened Mouth of the Wolf by introducing himself as my husband, before exploring my wrongful conviction and my confrontation with my prosecutor. As my partner, he could not pretend to be objective, and so he owned his subjectivity from the start. Essayists, too, should acknowledge any potentially relevant context that might inform how their writing is received, and in that spirit, I will share this: About a month before Fielder showed up to interview Holmes and Evans, I connected with the couple over Zoom. Holmes was preparing to go to prison and wanted advice on what to expect and how to hold her family together. I did not need to have an opinion on her guilt or innocence to offer whatever wisdom I had about the painful journey ahead. I don’t think that information compromises the integrity of this essay, but revealing it gives you more context to make your own judgments. What has made the shallowness of this whole debate about Evans’s profit-sharing request so strange, for me, is that no one understands better than Fielder that objectivity is a fiction. Across all of his major works— Nathan for You , The Rehearsal , The Curse —Fielder deconstructs the myth of neutrality, exposing how human bias or the presence of a camera inevitably distorts reality. That project is one of the things I most admire about You Can See Everything . Holmes and Evans invite a crew to live with them as an act of radical transparency, and Fielder, suspecting that their transparency is a performance, delivers his own performance of radical transparency. Every cut is intended to shape what you, the audience, should think and feel. That thin, ominous string note playing under Evans and Holmes’s meet-cute story is meant to manipulate you. No matter how much Fielder pulls back the curtain, it’s still a performance. All filmmakers have a point of view, and Fielder has built a career on exposing that fact. So I found it strange that this story about money is the only one he asks viewers to take on faith, without ever interrogating their first assumptions. When Evans pointed out that other documentary subjects have been paid, citing the Sussexes’ deal with Netflix that resulted in the Harry & Meghan series, Oppenheim brushed the comparison aside, saying, “That’s not a real documentary.” What is a “real documentary”? An objective one? You can’t spend three hours showing that objectivity is a pose and then argue that paying the subject would compromise the film’s objectivity. You Can See Everything earned $15 million in its opening weekend. A24 made money. Fielder and Oppenheim made money. When Fielder first objected to Evans’s request, he did so on the grounds that it was unethical. Later, he argued that it made the couple look greedy. When his pressure campaign worked and Evans forfeited his share—expanding the pool of profits available to the film’s other stakeholders—the film cast Evans and Holmes as greedy and suspicious anyway. Which only goes to show that Evans never had a say in what mattered most: creative control over the film itself. Five years ago, I wrote for The Atlantic about the ways my name, my face, and my story have been used without my consent: the Lifetime movie made while I was still in prison; the network drama pitched as “What if Amanda Knox became a lawyer?”; the Matt Damon film, Stillwater , that fictionalized away my innocence. My essay was about consent. I said very little about money. I should have said more, because the flow of money reveals whom a story truly belongs to. This was made clear to me in 2021, when my husband and I introduced our newborn daughter to the world through a feature in The New York Times . We knew that the tabloids would send paparazzi out for photos of me with babe in arms, and publish stories saying what it meant for the notorious murder suspect Amanda Knox to give birth. We wanted to tell our own story first, on our own terms. So we sat for a long interview in which I talked about new motherhood and the invasions of my private life, and we gave the Times exclusive photos of me holding our daughter, her face turned away from the camera. Soon after, that photo—and another from the shoot that the Times had not published—appeared in the Daily Mail alongside an article accusing me of duplicity for not revealing my daughter’s birth on the day she was born, as if I owed that information to the world. I was shocked, furious, confused. Had the Times been hacked? We ran it up the chain as high as we could, looking for answers, until the executive editor reached out to us. He told us that he took our child’s privacy seriously, and that the photos had now been removed from the Redux database that had made them available to license to whoever paid. When asked to comment by The Atlantic , a spokesperson for the Times described such licensing as “common practice for news organizations.” The Times would never, because of journalistic integrity, pay a source for an interview or a photograph. And yet it sold pictures of my infant to a tabloid in direct violation of my stated desires. [ Amanda Knox: My last trial ] I bring this up not out of spite for The New York Times . I bring it up to point out that even “ethical” media are entangled with “unethical” media, and that who gets paid is a poor measure of what makes a piece of journalism ethical. I’m getting paid to write this. I’m guessing you’d feel weird if I told you I was kicking Billy Evans a share. (I’m not.) We have strong intuitions about such things, but they aren’t always reliable guides. A norm against “checkbook journalism” makes sense; you can’t hold truth to power when you have to pay power for access. But that standard collapses when a “public figure” has less power than the journalists dissecting her. Being wrongly accused of murder did not make me powerful, but it did limit my right to privacy. There are no contextual rules or expiration to public figuredom, so I have no legal recourse when TMZ stakes out my wedding. Even musicians and movie stars, who have immense cultural influence, have zero power to stop paparazzi from hounding them. In Holmes’s case, she is a publicly disgraced convicted criminal who has been ordered to pay back $452 million. Who has more power, her and Evans, or A24, Fielder, and Oppenheim? That power differential matters to the question of how ethics, money, and objectivity should be judged in a documentary film. I doubt there exists a perfect system that balances the public’s need—or at least desire—to know about people in the news, and those people’s right to protect their own privacy or profit from their own exposure. What I do know is that, in a more ethical system, a subject who agrees to give journalists exclusive access should have some say over where her images wind up. And if a family agrees to let a documentarian into their home, no one should think it’s strange for them to want something in return. “Traditional journalistic standards” don’t ensure that a documentary film is objective. They merely ensure that the person in front of the camera is the only one whose financial incentives are not shaping the outcome.

items.title: Tunisie | La crise de tomate risque de perdurer
items.description: Alors que les consommateurs se plaignent de la pénurie et de la hausse du prix des tomates sur le marché, la Fédération régionale des producteurs de tomates destinées à la transformation, dans le gouvernorat de Nabeul, premier pôle de production et de transformation (représentant environ 27 % à 32 % de la superficie/production), a appelé les producteurs de la région à boycotter la culture de la tomate pour la saison 2027. Si la menace est mise à exécution cela n’améliorera guère la situation. Les producteurs de tomates ont pris cette décision en signe de protestation contre l’aggravation des problèmes structurels affectant les filières de production et de transformation. C’est ce qu’a indiqué le secrétaire général de la Fédération, Mohamed Ben Hassen, sur les ondes de Diwan FM , justifiant cet appel au boycott par les difficultés rencontrées par les agriculteurs, notamment la hausse persistante des coûts de production, la pénurie de main-d’œuvre, ainsi que le coût élevé des plants, dont certains ne répondent pas aux normes requises. M. Ben Hassen a dénoncé ce qu’il considère comme un déséquilibre dans la répartition des charges et des bénéfices entre les différents maillons de la filière, critiquant, au passage, l’augmentation, à partir de septembre 2026, du prix de la boîte de concentré de tomate (format 800 g) de 660 millimes, alors que le prix d’achat de la tomate auprès de l’agriculteur reste bloqué à 270 millimes le kilogramme, sans aucune révision depuis quatre ans. Le responsable syndical a, par ailleurs, indiqué que, selon les prévisions de production déclarées, le stock total de concentré de tomate atteindra environ 70 000 tonnes en juin 2027, couvrant ainsi plus de 70 % de la consommation locale pour la saison à venir. Il a insisté sur l’urgence d’une intervention pour réorganiser le secteur et instaurer un équilibre juste, garantissant les droits de l’agriculteur — désormais le maillon le plus faible de la chaîne — malgré son rôle fondamental dans la sécurité alimentaire et le soutien à l’économie nationale. Il est à rappeler que la Tunisie est l’un des pays producteurs et transformateurs de tomates les plus importants au monde (souvent classée dans le top 10 mondial pour la transformation), mais le secteur traverse une période de turbulences économiques en 2026 en raison de déséquilibres entre les coûts de production, les prix de référence et l’accumulation des stocks. Lors de la campagne agricole 2026, la production de tomates a atteint environ 1,1 million de tonnes, réparties comme suit : 200 000 tonnes pour la consommation en frais, 60 000 tonnes pour le séchage et 840 000 tonnes pour la transformation industrielle. I. B. L’article Tunisie | La crise de tomate risque de perdurer est apparu en premier sur Kapitalis .

items.title: Megaspeed says Alice Huang left the company in August 2025
items.description: Megaspeed said on Sunday that Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang, whose ties to former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang have raised US national security concerns, officially left the company on August 30, 2025, and has no current role there. The Singapore-based cloud-computing company is an Nvidia business partner in the Asia-Pacific region and has been in the spotlight after reports that Jensen Huang had an affair with former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, whom US authorities suspect of being a Chinese spy. “Megaspeed does not comment on Ms Huang’s personal and private matters,” the company’s statement added. In October 2025, the New York Times reported that Megaspeed was under US investigation over whether it helped Chinese customers obtain Nvidia computer chips subject to Washington’s export controls. China has denied the allegation, and Megaspeed has not been found to have violated ​the rules. “Megaspeed is aware of recent media reports containing assertions about our business, supply chain and global operations that are not supported by verifiable evidence,” it said in Sunday’s statement. The company said it conducted “legitimate and lawful business” and had retained external legal counsel to conduct a thorough internal investigation. It added that its operations and supply chain controls were designed to comply with applicable laws and regulations, including US export-control requirements. Alice Huang became the controlling shareholder of Megaspeed in March 2023, according to Washington-based research group C4ADS, which reviewed corporate records. The US government and Nvidia did not respond immediately to Reuters requests for comment on Megaspeed’s statement.

items.title: PM Shehbaz, CDF Munir share top spot in list of world’s 500 most influential Muslims
items.description: Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif and Chief of Defence Forces and Chief of the Army Staff Field Marshal Asim Munir have shared the top spot in the latest edition of the world’s 500 most influential Muslims, alongside the Saudi king and crown prince and the Turkish president. The rankings have been compiled by the Royal Islamic Strategic Studies Centre (RISSC), a research institute based in Amman, Jordan. It has been publishing an annual report titled “The 500 Most Influential Muslims” since 2009, recognising and highlighting individuals who have made significant contributions to Muslim communities. This is the first time that the list features multiple names for the top rank, recognising the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement between Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye, according to the edition. “While this unified top spot features five individuals, it is actually divided into three shared entries that represent a massive shift in how Muslim nations are working together to protect one another. The main reason for this historic decision is the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement,” the edition said. It added, “This mutual-defence pact unites the immense wealth of Saudi Arabia, the advanced tech and manufacturing of Turkiye, and the powerful military strength of Pakistan into a collective alliance. “Modelled on a ‘one for all, all for one’ approach to security, this pact has completely reshaped regional politics.” The report also acknowledged that “over the past year, Pakistan has navigated an intricate set of economic stabilisation challenges, regional security pressures, and major-power diplomatic balancing acts”. It noted that Islamabad engaged in “regional shuttle diplomacy” in the Middle East to advocate for de-escalation, “even as domestic energy markets faced immediate pressures via elevated import costs and emergency fuel conservation measures”. Information Minister Attaullah Tarar posted about the development on X, saying, “A moment of gratitude for every Pakistani.” He added, “From Marka-i-Haq to global diplomacy, they walked this journey together. This honour is a tribute to the sacrifices of our martyrs and the unity of our nation.” Following the leaders of Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye, at the fourth and fifth place in the list are Iranian Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei and Jordan’s King Abdullah II, respectively. Qatar’s Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al-Thani is ranked at number six while United Arab Emirates President Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al-Nahyan has been ranked at number 12. Egyptian President Abdel Fattah Saeed El-Sisi is at number 22. Pakistani Scholar Sheikh Muhammad Taqi Usmani has been listed as the seventh most influential Muslim, while Scholar Maulana Tariq Jamil is ranked at 32. Footballer Mohamed Salah is ranked at 39. Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas is listed at number 45, followed by Syrian Interim President Ahmed Al-Sharaa at the 46th place. New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani is listed as the 49th most influential Muslim in the list. Honourable mentions in politics include Hamas Chief Khalil Al-Hayya, former prime minister Imran Khan, London Mayor Sadiq Khan and American Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed . Similarly, honourable mentions in the “Social Issues, Science, Arts & Culture, Media and Sports” category include Jordan’s Queen Rania Al-Abdullah, British composer Sami Yusuf, Palestinian journalist Bisan Owda, British-American broadcaster and journalist Mehdi Hasan and Egyptian comedian Bassem Youssef. Every year, the RISSC also names two people as Man of the Year and Woman of the Year. This year, Palestinian paediatrician Dr Hussam Abu Safiya has been named as the Man of the Year. He is described as “a doctor who refused to abandon his patients, buried his son and returned to the wards, and has now spent more than six hundred days in Israeli custody without charge or trial”. Under Israel’s invasion of Gaza, he documented attacks on medical facilities and appealed to the international community to protect Gaza’s health infrastructure. “A man with no army, no office and no freedom has done more than most governments to remind the world what courage and integrity look like,” the report says. Minab school attack survivor Fatemeh Zahra Sheikhabadi has been honoured as the Woman of the Year. On Feb 28, a US missile struck an elementary girls school in Iran’s Minab, killing over 150 people, including over 100 children. After surviving the US strikes on her school, Sheikhabadi travelled to Geneva and addressed the UN Human Rights Council, urging world leaders to “hear the voices of the children of Minab”, the report says. “She is honoured not as a symbol of a war, but as herself: a girl who lost her friends and her teachers on an ordinary morning, and who lived to tell their story so that it would not be lost with them,” the report added.

items.title: Le ministère de la Santé et de l’Hygiène publique et Sénégal Solidaire unissent leurs efforts autour de la vaccination
items.description: La prévention du cancer du col de l’utérus passe notamment par une meilleure adhésion des populations à la vaccination contre le papillomavirus humain (HPV). Dans cette perspective, le ministère de la Santé et de l’Hygiène publique entend renforcer sa collaboration avec la Fondation nationale Sénégal Solidaire, en misant davantage sur la sensibilisation et la mobilisation communautaire. Une délégation du ministère de la Santé et de l’Hygiène publique , conduite par la directrice de Cabinet du ministre, Dr Ndèye Magatte Ndome Ndiaye, a rencontré les responsables de la Fondation nationale Sénégal Solidaire, en présence de la Première Dame, Absa Faye, ambassadrice de cette organisation. Au cœur des échanges, les défis liés à la vaccination contre le HPV, notamment l’adhésion des populations, mais aussi la nécessité d’intensifier les actions de communication et de proximité pour favoriser le recours à cette mesure préventive. À cette occasion, la Première Dame a proposé d’intégrer la vaccination contre le HPV aux initiatives du programme « Octobre Rose toute l’année ». Une démarche qui vise à inscrire la prévention du cancer du col de l’utérus dans une dynamique continue, au-delà des campagnes ponctuelles de sensibilisation. Elle a également préconisé une mobilisation accrue des différents acteurs engagés dans la lutte contre les cancers féminins. A.N

items.title: Blasts rattle Bahrain as Iran launches second drone attack in 3 days
items.description: Blasts echoed over Bahrain on Sunday as the tiny Gulf nation was rattled by the second Iranian drone attack in three days, ending a long lull in strikes during the Middle East war . Sirens rang out, and authorities posted several alerts on social media urging residents to seek shelter, their first warnings since September. Iran’s Revolutionary Guards said they carried out a drone attack on a US radar system in the desert island state, which hosts US military facilities including a major naval base. Bahrain’s military said it intercepted the attacks, “preventing them from reaching their intended targets”. The foreign ministry said air defence systems shot down Iranian drones. “It’s exactly what I was hoping wouldn’t happen: Iranian attacks starting again, with all the worry and uncertainty that go with them,” resident Hayat Ibrahim, 65, told AFP . Iran also fired drones at Bahrain on Friday — the first strikes since September against countries in the energy-rich Gulf, which has been heavily targeted in the eight-month war. Explosions could be heard around 4am (6am PKT) on Sunday, an AFP journalist said, with residents reporting a second series of blasts around 6:30am. The interior ministry, posting on X , called on “residents to remain calm, proceed to the nearest safe location, and follow news through official channels”. Mohammed Abdallah, a shopkeeper in the capital, Manama, heard the strikes overnight. “I was hoping this period was behind us and wouldn’t happen again,” he said. ‘Settling scores’ Iran’s Revolutionary Guards said the drones targeted a US radar system at a helicopter base, according to a statement carried by the Iranian state broadcaster. “The US air defence radar system at the Al-Riffa helicopter base in Bahrain was targeted by six drones belonging to the IRGC Aerospace Force,” the Guards said in a statement posted by the state broadcaster on Telegram. “The Strait of Hormuz is closed, and any aggression by the American enemy will be met with an even harsher and more forceful response,” it added. Bahrain “rejects turning its territory into an arena for settling scores and holds Iran fully responsible for these attacks”, a foreign ministry statement said. During more than eight months of war, Iran has restricted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz oil trade route and struck infrastructure including airports, seaports, energy facilities, and US assets across the region. The Gulf countries have weathered thousands of Iranian drones and missiles since the war began on February 28. On Friday, following this month’s US strikes on Qeshm island in Hormuz, the Revolutionary Guards said their forces targeted a US early warning radar system in Bahrain. The US military’s Central Command (Centcom) said it shot down two Iranian drones in Friday’s attack, reporting no casualties or damage. Centcom, which oversees American military operations in the region, said last month that it had helped Gulf countries export 1.5 billion barrels of oil since the summer via Hormuz. US President Donald Trump, whose steep reverse in midterm elections was partly blamed on the Iran war, plans to discuss the conflict at a trilateral meeting with his Chinese and Russian counterparts this week, an official said Friday. Months of diplomacy have failed to resolve the war, which began with surprise US-Israeli strikes that assassinated Iran’s supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei.

items.title: La ministre des Finances va-t-elle fouiller dans les poches des Tunisiens ?
items.description: Je ne m’attendais pas à devoir attendre mon retour en Tunisie pour commenter cette déclaration. Alors que j’étais pleinement concentré, en train de suivre les travaux d’un forum international à Shanghai, mes pensées ont été interrompues par les propos de la ministre des Finances, Mechket Salama Khaldi. Elle appelle les Tunisiens à sortir ce qu’ils ont dans leurs poches — et à révéler l’argent qu’ils dissimulent — afin de contribuer aux ressources de l’État ! Ridha Chkondali * Honnêtement, je ne vois pas dans cette déclaration un simple appel à mobiliser des ressources supplémentaires ; j’y perçois plutôt une réduction inquiétante de la crise financière et économique que traverse le pays à une seule question : comment extraire davantage d’argent des poches des citoyens ? La ministre des Finances ignore-t-elle qu’il existe des lois économiques et historiques selon lesquelles une pression fiscale excessive ne conduit pas nécessairement à une augmentation des ressources de l'État ? Au contraire, elle risque d’affaiblir l’activité économique, de freiner l’investissement et l’épargne, de favoriser l’évasion fiscale et, in fine, de réduire l’assiette fiscale elle-même. L’épargne des ménages en chute libre Ne sait-elle pas qu’Ibn Khaldoun avait déjà souligné, il y a des siècles, l’existence — à certaines étapes — d’une relation inverse entre l’alourdissement de la charge fiscale et le rendement des recettes fiscales ? Mais, avant d’exiger des Tunisiens qu’ils sortent l’argent qu’ils dissimulent, ne serait-il pas plus pertinent de se demander : que leur reste-t-il, au juste, à dissimuler ? La capacité d’épargne des Tunisiens a chuté à des niveaux préoccupants. Selon les données de l’Institut national de la statistique, le taux d’épargne des ménages n’a pas dépassé 3 % en 2025, contre 8,6 % en 2021. L’inflation alimentaire et la hausse des prix des produits de première nécessité ont-elles laissé la moindre marge financière aux familles ? La ministre des Finances sait-elle quelle part du revenu des ménages est désormais consacrée à l’alimentation ? Et combien de familles tunisiennes en sont réduites à dépenser la totalité de leurs revenus, voire à s’endetter, pour subvenir à leurs besoins essentiels ? Qu’a fait l'État de toutes ces ressources qu’il a mobilisées ? Par ailleurs, une question majeure, incontournable, se pose : qu’a fait l'État de toutes ces ressources mobilisées et de tous ces fonds captés auprès du secteur privé ? Où sont passés les prêts et les financements qui ont détourné des ressources — initialement destinées au financement des entreprises et à l’investissement privé — vers la couverture des besoins du Trésor public ? La ministre des Finances ignore-t-elle que la Banque centrale a injecté, selon les estimations qui circulent, environ 25 milliards de dinars en trois ans pour financer les besoins de l’État ? Et quel a été le bilan en matière de développement de cette mobilisation exceptionnelle ? A-t-on constaté une amélioration tangible des services de santé et des prestations sociales ? Les infrastructures, les transports publics et le réseau routier se sont-ils améliorés ? A-t-on assisté à une véritable réforme des entreprises publiques qui drainent les ressources de l’État ? Le système de subventions a-t-il été réformé pour mieux cibler les véritables bénéficiaires ? Les déséquilibres structurels de la fonction publique ont-ils été corrigés ? Le climat des affaires s’est-il amélioré, permettant aux investisseurs d’être plus confiants quant à l’avenir de leurs investissements ? L’économie parallèle a-t-elle été combattue et intégrée au circuit économique formel ? Où sont donc les réformes qui auraient dû précéder toute nouvelle exigence de sacrifices ? Le citoyen, l’investisseur et le secteur privé dans le collimateur Au lieu de cela, nous sommes confrontés à un discours qui fait peser sur le citoyen, l’investisseur et le secteur privé la responsabilité de fournir des ressources supplémentaires à l’État, sans pour autant apporter de réponses convaincantes sur la gestion des ressources précédentes, ni proposer une vision claire pour remédier aux déséquilibres structurels des finances publiques. L’État n’est pas qu’une simple caisse nécessitant constamment davantage de fonds pour combler son déficit. L’État, c’est un ensemble d’institutions, de services, d’investissements, de développement et de confiance. Il est inacceptable que la fiscalité — conçue à l’origine comme un levier pour financer le développement et assurer les services publics — se transforme en une fin en soi, et que le succès de la politique financière soit désormais mesuré à la seule capacité à extraire toujours plus de fonds des citoyens et des entreprises. L’enjeu n’est pas de traquer l’argent que les Tunisiens pourraient dissimuler, mais de comprendre pourquoi ils ont perdu confiance dans l’investissement et l’épargne ; d’analyser les politiques qui ont conduit l’État à concurrencer le secteur privé pour l’accès aux ressources financières ; et d’identifier les réformes qui, malgré les lourds sacrifices consentis par le pays, n’ont toujours pas été réalisées. Les citoyens ne sont pas une réserve pour éponger le déficit de l’Etat Madame la ministre des Finances, avant de demander aux Tunisiens de vider leurs poches, présentez-nous le bilan des réformes menées par votre ministère et par le gouvernement. Les Tunisiens ne sont pas une réserve de secours pour éponger le déficit budgétaire ; le secteur privé n’est pas une machine à financer les dépenses publiques ; et la fiscalité ne saurait se substituer à la croissance, à la production et à l’investissement. Épuiser la capacité d’épargne des citoyens, fragiliser les entreprises et marginaliser l’investissement ne permettra jamais de bâtir un État fort, quand bien même les recettes fiscales augmenteraient temporairement. L’État, qui cherche constamment à puiser dans les poches de ses citoyens, devrait d’abord rechercher les causes de son propre déficit dans ses choix économiques et financiers. C’est à cette question que la ministre des Finances devrait répondre, plutôt que de demander aux Tunisiens de sortir ce qu’il leur reste dans les poches ! Que Dieu te vienne en aide, Tunisie ! Traduit de l’arabe. * Expert économique. L’article La ministre des Finances va-t-elle fouiller dans les poches des Tunisiens ? est apparu en premier sur Kapitalis .
